The White amur bream Parabramis pekinensis, a cyprinid native to the Amur River basin and adjacent waters of eastern Asia, exhibits a life history typical of many potamodromous, benthopelagic Cypriniformes. Maximum recorded body lengths for this species approach 55 centimeters [Li = 55 centimeters], a size class that places it among the larger members of its genus. Neonatal mass is exceedingly small, with newly hatched yolk-sac larvae weighing approximately 0.001 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.001 grams], a value consistent with the minute, pelagic eggs characteristic of many cyprinids. This tiny starting size is offset by a rapid growth trajectory during the first several months of life, during which the exogenously feeding larva transitions through the larval metamorphosis and into the juvenile stage. The species is known to form large aggregations in slow-moving river reaches and floodplain lakes, where it feeds predominantly on aquatic vegetation, detritus, and occasional zooplankton. Comparative data from related species within the subfamily Cultrinae suggest that this combination of high fecundity and small offspring size is an adaptation to variable environmental conditions in temperate floodplain habitats.

Reproductive maturation in Parabramis pekinensis occurs at a total length of approximately 35 centimeters [Lp = approximately 35 centimeters], a threshold that corresponds to the onset of gonadal recrudescence and the first spawning event for most individuals in wild populations. At this pubertal length, the corresponding wet body mass is roughly 556 grams [Wwp = roughly 556 grams], indicating that considerable somatic growth must be completed before reproductive investment begins. The attainment of this developmental milestone is governed by both thermal and photoperiodic cues typical of temperate latitudes, with spawning runs typically commencing in late spring when water temperatures rise. Field observations indicate that first reproduction generally occurs during the third or fourth year of life, depending on local growing season length and food availability. The shift from an immature, growing juvenile to a reproductively viable adult is accompanied by pronounced changes in gonad morphology and elevated circulating levels of sex steroids. This timing of maturation is broadly similar to that reported for other medium-bodied cyprinids in the Amur basin, although local variation in growth rates can shift the age at which this length is attained by as much as a year.

Body mass at the asymptotic or ultimate adult stage reaches approximately 2215 grams [Wwi = approximately 2215 grams] in Parabramis pekinensis, a size that is typically achieved after several years of sustained feeding and growth in productive lentic environments. At this mass, individuals are considered to be at their physiological maximum, having completed the majority of their somatic expansion. This ultimate wet weight represents a near tenfold increase over the mass at puberty and underscores the substantial post-maturation growth that this species continues to exhibit. Such continued size increase after reproductive onset is characteristic of indeterminate growers and allows larger, older females to contribute disproportionately to annual egg production through increased fecundity and egg size. The relationship between length and mass in this species follows a power-law curve typical of cyprinids, with larger individuals displaying a somewhat deeper body shape. Maximum longevity in natural populations has been estimated at 17 years under the thermal regime of the Amur River at 16 °C [T = 16 °C], corresponding to a lifespan of 6205 days [am = 6205 days] based on field mark-recapture studies.

Reproductive output in Parabramis pekinensis is seasonally concentrated, with females depositing their eggs in adhesive batches on submerged vegetation in shallow, well-oxygenated habitats. The maximum daily reproduction rate has been estimated at approximately 241 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 241 eggs per day] when females are maintained at 16 °C [T = 16 °C], a figure derived from the product of mean clutch size and spawning frequency during the peak reproductive window. This calculation arises from an annual fecundity of roughly 88,000 eggs per year [Ri = roughly 88,000 eggs per year], which is partitioned across a spawning season lasting several months. Females are capable of releasing multiple clutches over the course of a single breeding period, with the interval between successive spawning events influenced by water temperature and the availability of suitable spawning substrate. Such iteroparous reproductive strategy buffers the population against the risk of complete reproductive failure in any given year, a common feature of cyprinids inhabiting hydrologically unpredictable floodplain systems.

At 16 °C [T = 16 °C], the thermal regime typical of the main growing season in the middle Amur River, Parabramis pekinensis exhibits a lifespan of 17 years [am = 17 years], representing an extended period of reproductive opportunity for this medium-sized cyprinid. This longevity, coupled with an asymptotic total length of 55 centimeters [Li = 55 centimeters], allows individuals to accumulate substantial reproductive output over their lifetimes. The species' life history strategy thus combines moderate size at maturity with high fecundity and a protracted reproductive window, a suite of traits that appears well-suited to the seasonally dynamic, food-rich environments of East Asian floodplain rivers. Comparative analysis with other Cultrinae reveals that the ultimate wet weight of 2215 grams [Wwi = 2215 grams] is near the upper end of the range for the subfamily, while the small neonate mass of 0.001 grams [Wwb = 0.001 grams] is typical. Future work should examine how ongoing climate warming may alter the thermal regime of the Amur basin and thereby shift the age-specific schedules of growth, maturation, and mortality in this economically important species.
